title: A new generation of vehicle routing research: robust algorithms, addressing uncertainty
contribution: Survey with Simchi-Levi of the worst-case and probabilistic analysis of vehicle routing: the radial-dominated asymptotic structure of optimal solutions, heuristic classes that can never be asymptotically optimal, an asymptotically optimal location-based heuristic built from that structure, why the set-partitioning LP is tight, a priori optimization for stochastic demand, and queueing-plus-geometry bounds and policies for the dynamic traveling repairman problem.
problem_entry: SD+AP (IO as engine): VRP heuristics tuned on standard test problems lack robustness and are data-sensitive (Fisher 1995), so analysis should give 'robust' algorithms independent of the data environment (pp. 1-2); classical static models have little to say once demand is stochastic and dynamic (pp. 2, 13).
key_idea: Analysis first: the asymptotic optimal cost is radial-dominated (2nE(d)/q; 2n*gamma*E(d)), which condemns route-first/cluster-second heuristics (next-fit constant) and yields the asymptotically optimal location-based heuristic; a priori sequences replace daily re-optimization; the DTRP is a median location problem in light traffic and TSP batching in heavy traffic (pp. 3-7, 10, 14-16).
assumptions: Symmetric triangle-inequality distances; i.i.d. planar locations with compact support and i.i.d. demands independent of location; known independent discrete demand distributions (SVRP); renewal arrivals, continuous spatial density, i.i.d. service times with two finite moments (DTRP); asymptotic almost-sure results with proofs left to handbook chapters ('intuitive level'); no data (pp. 2-4, 11, 14).
proof_devices: Matching asymptotic upper and lower bounds; grid region-partitioning upper bound with cells shrinking more slowly than n grows (pp. 3-4)
Heuristic class mapped to next-fit bin packing via Rhee-Talagrand constants, so no member is asymptotically optimal (p. 5)
Upper-bound construction of the asymptotic proof turned into an algorithm: LBH as capacitated concentrator location solved by Lagrangian relaxation (pp. 6-7)
Asymptotic tightness of the set-partitioning LP relaxation explains column generation; other formulations can diverge (Theorem 12, pp. 8-9)
Worst-case ratios with tight examples for a priori heuristics: cyclic 1+alpha, space-filling curve O(log n) (pp. 11-12)
Polynomial evaluation of a priori expected length against the (K+1)^n-term re-optimization expectation (p. 11)

DTRP lower bounds for all stable policies plus attaining TSP policies: stability iff rho<1, 1/(1-rho)^2 growth, fourfold gain from doubling the fleet, factor about 1.8 conjectured to be lower-bound slack (pp. 14-16)
experiments: none new (survey); others' evidence reported in one line each: hierarchical design within 35% of a lower bound at 100 customers and 16% at 500, exact SVRP up to 50 nodes, 'extensive computational results' for a priori strategies, simulated DTRP constants; no instances, solvers or run times (pp. 7-9, 12, 15, 17).
positioning: Against the empirical heuristic-tuning tradition (Fisher 1995) and against small-scale stochastic programming for random demand ('completely different'); continues Beardwood-Halton-Hammersley, Haimovich-Rinnooy Kan, Rhee-Talagrand and the Jaillet / Bertsimas-Jaillet-Odoni a priori line; answers Psaraftis's remark that routing and congestion theory had not been combined (pp. 1, 3-5, 10, 13).
writing: Survey register: theorem then an 'intuitively' paragraph, Reflections subsections, a four-point summary opening 'We believe'; a referee's practice caveat printed in the summary, followed by 'We hope'; practice examples (UPS, bank cash, utility repair, car haulers) lead the uncertainty sections (pp. 3-6, 10-13, 17).
limits_future: Proofs omitted (p. 2); hierarchical design may converge slowly (p. 9); heavy-traffic optimality of TSP policies only conjectured (p. 15); referee: travel-time variation and crew scheduling complicate practice (p. 17); a priori optimization recommended where computing is scarce (pp. 12, 17); no future-work list. 'Robust' means data-environment independence shown by analysis, not uncertainty sets (p. 1).

method_links.note: Problems owned by other traditions (empirical VRP heuristics, stochastic programming, queueing) re-entered through combinatorial optimization plus probability: VRP recast as concentrator location, set-partitioning LP asymptotically exact, boundary printed (re-optimization expectation intractable, a priori cost computable); the device is asymptotic analysis, not a formulation kept in a solver class.

Two precursors of the price of X: price of fairness (spatially unbiased vs biased DTRP policies with closed-form bounds, zero gap under uniform demand) and price of simplicity (a priori vs re-optimization; nearest-neighbour-started cyclic heuristic asymptotically equal in the capacitated case); set size n as one knob for travel cost vs waiting time; no curve or solution-independent probability bound.

Mirror image of the 'why now': in 1996 scarce computation justifies a priori routes over re-optimization; method choice is indexed to available computation, in the opposite direction from the 2014+ argument for exact MIO.

Practice supplies the settings and the objective (waiting time over distance for five stated reasons) and operational reasons justify a priori routes (computing, redesign time, driver confusion, regular service), but no owner's current rule, data or decision metric is used.

title: On the worst case complexity of potential reduction algorithms for linear programming
contribution: Shows that the O(sqrt(n) L) iteration bound of Ye's potential-reduction interior-point algorithm (and of Freund's and Gonzaga-Todd's variants) is tight even with exact line searches and on network-structured LPs, via an instance needing Omega((sqrt(n)/nu) log(1/eps)) primal steps for q = 2n + nu*sqrt(n).
problem_entry: LO: potential-reduction IPMs combine the best known O(sqrt(n) L) bound with practical line searches, 'a rare combination'; four numbered questions ask whether the bound is inherent in the algorithm or the proof, whether line searches or network structure help, and whether it is inherent in LP; the first three are answered negatively (pp. 1-3).
key_idea: A lower-bound instance, not a new algorithm: a two-chain network LP (x_i = x_{i+1}, b = 0, c = e) whose iterates stay in a two-value symmetric family, started at the ratio for which the exact line-search step repeats forever, so each primal step cuts the gap only by 1/(1 + nu/sqrt(n)) (pp. 6-12).
assumptions: Standard-form LP; Tanabe-Todd-Ye primal-dual potential with parameter q; Ye's Algorithm A with exact line search on primal steps; a deliberately degenerate instance (optimal value 0, unique primal optimum at zero, every dual feasible point optimal) and one specified starting point; no data (pp. 2-6, 9, 11).
proof_devices: Symmetry: projection matrix independent of k, iterates take only two values r^k, t^k (Proposition 1, pp. 7-8)
Exact line-search step depends only on r/t and satisfies g(r/t) = g(t/r); unique minimizer by a second-derivative argument (Proposition 2, pp. 8-9)
Fixed point of the ratio-flip map forces the same step alpha* every iteration: omega* = nu/sqrt(n), alpha* = (2 + nu/sqrt(n))/(1 + nu/sqrt(n))^2 (pp. 9-10)
Induction plus per-step gap reduction 1/(1 + nu/sqrt(n)) from an initial gap of 2n + nu*sqrt(n) gives the step count; q = 2n + Theta(sqrt(n)) gives Omega(sqrt(n) log(1/eps)) (pp. 11-12)
b = 0 makes the gap c'x so dual steps do not move it; primal steps dominate work, so a primal-step bound bounds time (pp. 6, 12)
positioning: Within IPM complexity: Karmarkar O(nL), path-following O(sqrt(n) L) with impractical small steps, Ye's potential reduction as the practical route; prior lower bounds by Anstreicher, Kaliski-Ye, Powell, Todd and Todd-Ye. Three guest members appear: Ye (algorithm studied, draft comments acknowledged), Nesterov (long-step method possibly escaping the bound), Powell (Karmarkar lower bound cited) (pp. 2-4, 12-13).
writing: Abstract frames 'a significant open question' and 'some negative answers'; four numbered questions answered by number; question 4 called 'rather deep'; three reasons (a)-(c) why the bound is strong; 13 pages, no figures; uncovered algorithms listed by reference number (pp. 1-3, 6, 12).
limits_future: One instance and one starting point; possibly not covering Kojima-Mizuno-Yoshise, Nesterov's long-step, Ye's projective and Ye et al.; q = n + nu*sqrt(n) with nu = Omega(sqrt(n)) open; future: 'a general lower bound for all potential reduction algorithms'; question 4 (inherent in LP) untouched (pp. 11-12).

method_links.note: Tractability in the 1997 complexity-class sense: prints where an algorithm's guarantee ends (tight Omega(sqrt(n) log(1/eps))) with no solve time at all, the far end of the drift from complexity class to solve time recorded in Method 1's Limitations [02 C2]; by the later Research Taste it falls under warning sign 2 (polynomial time without solve times), though the class is motivated by practical line searches.

title: Optimal control of execution costs
contribution: Defines best execution as the solution of a stochastic dynamic program minimizing the expected cost of executing a block within T periods, derives closed-form linear policies and quadratic value functions (naive equal split optimal only under linear permanent impact and an arithmetic random walk; information and LPT temporary-impact cases), gives numerical DP/ADP routes, portfolio and constraint extensions, and Monte Carlo evidence against the naive rule.
problem_entry: SD+AP (finance): execution costs are large (Perold's 20% paper vs 2.5% actual), institutions split blocks into multi-day packages (Chan-Lakonishok), and the law requires best execution while 'no clear definition of best execution exists'; execution's dynamic nature was recognized only implicitly by practitioners (pp. 2-3).
key_idea: Minimize E[sum P_t S_t] subject to sum S_t = S-bar by Bellman recursion with the trade's own price impact in the law of motion; the naive split is optimal only in the linear permanent-impact random-walk case; serially correlated information adds a linear correction (trade into expected price rises); the LPT law keeps a linear policy and quadratic value and splits cost into Perold's paper cost plus implementation shortfall (pp. 3-12, 20-22).
assumptions: Discrete 30-minute periods (T = 13 per day); buy programme; risk-neutral expected cost; partial equilibrium; order type subsumed; known parameters; Section 2 dynamics flagged as empirically implausible and replaced by LPT 'for convenience' and non-negative prices; no data, all parameters calibrated; empirical work deferred to Bertsimas, Hummel & Lo (1998) (pp. 4-7, 12-13, 17-22, 38-42).
proof_devices: Bellman recursion with closed-form coefficient recursions proved by induction on k (Appendix A, pp. 44-47; a_k = (h/2)(1 + 1/(k+1)), p. 45)
Interpretation of each policy coefficient: trading into expected price rises when rho > 0; impact cost tends to h*S^2/2 as T grows (pp. 9, 11-12, 16)
LPT specification chosen so cost separates exactly into no-impact and impact terms (implementation shortfall) and the LQ structure survives (pp. 20-22)
Discretized DP cost accounting: O(KJN) memory, 800,000 evaluations per stage, 16 million in all, about 16 s (p. 28)
Approximate DP with least-squares quadratic value functions, exact for the quadratic cases (pp. 28-29)
Constraints make the value function piecewise quadratic with 3^k pieces (3,486,784,401 at T = 20) (p. 35)
Closed form under no-sales with multiplicative impact: threshold structure in the growth rate theta (wait if theta <= 1/2, naive if theta = 1, front-load if theta > 1) (pp. 36-37)
experiments: Simulation only, calibrated parameters, baseline = naive equal split. Single paths (100,000 shares, T = 20, P0 = $50): Table 1 3.79 expected / 18.29 realized cents/share improvement, Table 2 optimal loses 4.11 cents/share realized while winning in expectation (pp. 13-16). Monte Carlo 25 (c, rho) pairs x 50,000 paths with theoretical value, mean and standard errors (Table 4, pp. 23-24); 'unrealistic' negative costs at c = 0.01 (p. 25). Headline 3-5 cents/share, 25-40% (pp. 25, 43) is not a Table 4 row (c = 0.0025: 1.77-2.68; c = 0.005: 7.08-10.70 vs naive 13.31). Sell frequencies (Table 5) and risk decomposition (fundamental std 73.6 vs impact 0.18 cents/share; Table 6) (pp. 33-34, 39-40). No real data.
positioning: Dynamic optimization in finance is old (Merton, Samuelson) but novel for defining best execution; builds on Perold's implementation shortfall and microstructure price-impact evidence (Hausman-Lo-MacKinlay, Chan-Lakonishok, Holthausen et al.); grants expected-utility-with-transaction-costs models are 'the right one' but intractable; reduced-form defence against strategic models; ADP cited from Bertsekas (1995) (pp. 3, 5, 18, 21, 28, 41-42).
writing: Finance register with long footnoted literature lists; economic motivation for four pages before the model; illustrative Section 2 ('primarily illustrative examples') then realistic Section 3; a full Section 7 on limitations; modest close ('Our more modest goal'); hedges such as 'seem to suggest that in some cases'; multivariate LPT formulas withheld ('contact the authors') (pp. 1-5, 16, 25, 33, 37-43).
limits_future: Written: order type and urgency (two-stage second-best), four sources of risk with parameter error and non-stationarity set aside, risk neutrality vs expected utility, partial equilibrium (pp. 38-42). Unwritten or weak: no real-data test, omitted portfolio formulas (p. 33), the 25-40% headline. Future: two-stage order-type optimization, transaction costs in consumption-investment and equilibrium models (pp. 38, 43). Note 05 correction: LPT impact is temporary (pp. 20-21); risk neutrality is in Section 7.3 (p. 41).

method_links.note: Formulation first for a notion law and practice leave undefined; specifications chosen to stay linear-quadratic (linear policy, quadratic value); when constraints leave the class (3^k pieces) the device is changed, not the solver (discretization, ADP, static-optimization alternative), i.e. Method 1's stop rule in 1998 form; the class is dynamic programming, not LP/conic/MIO.

Baseline is the practitioners' rule ('a naive (and not uncommon) strategy'), the decision metric is execution cost in cents/share against it, and the value function is offered to dealers as a pricing benchmark; evidence is simulated with calibrated parameters only, no owner data or field test. Also Heuristic 1 (evidence, DP form): the model under which practice's rule is exactly optimal is found, then extended.

title: The air traffic flow management problem with enroute capacities
contribution: A 0-1 formulation of air traffic flow management with airport and en-route sector capacities, built on cumulative 'by time t' variables whose connectivity constraints are facets and whose LP relaxation was almost always integral; NP-hardness, extensions (runway coupling, hubs, banks, rerouting), LP-bound dominance over earlier ground-holding formulations, and integral optimal solutions on real FAA-scale instances up to 1,002 flights.
problem_entry: IO+AP (air transportation): delays cost U.S. airlines about $3 billion a year against $2-2.5 billion losses; the FAA uses first-come, first-served ground holds and controller-experience rerouting; ground-holding models ignore en-route sector capacities, a concurrent IP has weak relaxations, and rerouting was unaddressed (pp. 1-2, 9).
key_idea: Use w_fjt = 1 if flight f has reached sector j by time t: sector, airport and time connectivity become pairwise precedence inequalities that are facets, the arrive-once constraint telescopes to a fixed parameter, delays are linear, and the LP relaxation is almost always integral, reducing the IP to LP (pp. 2, 4-5, 10).
assumptions: Deterministic, static per-period capacities for departures, arrivals and sectors; known schedules, traversal and turnaround times, linear ground and air delay costs; 5- or 15-minute periods with time windows (D = 6 in the U.S. sizing); data: Vranas et al. ground-holding sets with generated departures, OAG and pseudo-OAG flights on a 4-airport network, two real FAA/OAG instances 'Nothing ... generated or hypothesized' (pp. 3-6, 11-13).
proof_devices: NP-hardness with unit capacities by reduction from job-shop scheduling (Theorem 1, pp. 7-8)
LP-bound dominance by nested relaxations in a common variable space: Z_VBO <= Z_TP <= Z_MAGHP (Proposition 1, p. 7; Appendix A, pp. 13-14)
Non-integrality by a two-flight counterexample with a determinant-2 submatrix and fractional optimum (Theorem 2, p. 10; Appendix B, pp. 14-15)

Facets of the connectivity inequalities by counting affinely independent points, MAGHP only under simplifying assumptions; TFMP half 'similar, but more algebraically involved' and not given (pp. 10, 15-17)
Analytic size estimate before computing: at most 300,000 variables and 688,320 constraints for a U.S. instance (pp. 5-6)
experiments: GAMS + CPLEXMIP 2.1 on a SPARCstation 10 model 41; five questions answered point by point. MAGHP on Vranas et al. data (1,000 and 3,000 flights, connectivity 0.2-0.8) at the infeasibility border: non-integral only at 1,000 flights/40% (4% and 2.2%); comparison with published 'Previous Results' (not a rerun), earlier LP faster at 3,000 flights but total time lower here (pp. 11-12). TFMP: 200 flights 234 s, 1,000 flights 436 s, all integral; Table VII objectives non-monotone (typo). Real instances: 18,733 vars/43,226 cons in 1,141 s; 69,497/151,662 in 29,920 s (about 8.3 h for an 8-hour horizon), integral (pp. 12-13). Limits: data and memory. No comparison with the FAA's FCFS rule.
positioning: Taxonomy SAGHP -> MAGHP -> TFMP -> TFMRP (deterministic/stochastic x static/dynamic), mostly Odoni's group; supersedes the authors' own Vranas-Bertsimas-Odoni 1994a formulation (stronger LP bound, no rounding heuristics); balanced on Lindsay et al. (weak relaxations but strengthening techniques), speculative on Helme; authority invoked: polyhedral combinatorics (pp. 2, 7).
writing: Abstract lists contributions (a)-(e) and its opening sentences reappear as the introduction; 'We feel that our work makes the following contributions' with five points; an 'Important Remark' on the variable choice; questions posed before and answered after the computations; closing metaphor of an optimization 'brain' for the FAA command center; hedges 'we believe', 'we feel', 'very optimistic' (pp. 1-2, 5, 11, 13).
limits_future: Written: deterministic and static; needs airline interaction (cancellation and substitution), dynamic updating, stochastic capacities; rerouting formulations untested; other facets not sought; size limited by data and memory (pp. 10-11, 13). Unwritten: TFMP facet proof omitted (p. 15), no comparison with FCFS. Future: other capacitated flow systems (manufacturing, ground transportation) (p. 13).

method_links.note: Formulation designed so the IP behaves like an LP: cumulative variables make connectivity constraints facets and LP relaxations almost always integral ('reduce the problem to efficiently solving large scale linear programming'); boundary printed: NP-hard and non-integral polyhedra.

Exact solves certified by LP integrality and a duel with the incumbent formulation (his own 1994 one) on integrality and time, with the incumbent's faster LP at 3,000 flights admitted; no heuristic warm start, and the duel uses published numbers rather than a rerun.

Owner (FAA command center) and current rules (FCFS ground holds, controller-experience rerouting) named and FAA data used unaltered, but decisions are never scored against FCFS and deployment questions are left open.

Step 3: an air-traffic thesis line inspired by his adviser Odoni (Vranas 1994, then Stock Patterson), funded by Draper and the FAA. Also Research Taste 'strong formulations' stated jointly in 1998 (p. 2), the early side of Tension T4.

Facets examined 'in order to obtain a deeper understanding of why this formulation performs so well computationally'; with S025 Theorem 12 (this batch).

transferable: Use cumulative 'by time t' binaries in time-indexed flow and scheduling IPs: precedence becomes w_{f,j',t+l} <= w_{f,j,t}, monotonicity w_{t-1} <= w_t, and the assignment equality a fixed parameter; these give facet-defining constraints (pp. 4-5, 10).

Prove LP-bound dominance over rival formulations by nesting their relaxations in a common variable space (pp. 7, 13-14).
Refute integrality with the smallest counterexample, then explain good computational behaviour by facets (pp. 10, 14-15).
Test at the infeasibility border and report the percentage of non-integral variables next to CPU time per instance (pp. 11-13).
